Question: For a catalyzed solid-fluid reaction, of the following possible actions, which one will not solve the deactivation of the catalyst that is caused by poisoning?

A. All of them are good options to solve catalyst deactivation
B. Improve feedback conditioning
C. Limit the transition-state shape selectivity
D. Operate at higher reaction temperatures
E. Use egg-shell catalyst particles

Thought: Let me analyze each option carefully:

A. "All of them are good options to solve catalyst deactivation" - This is a catch-all option claiming all other options work.

B. "Improve feedback conditioning" - This doesn't seem to be a standard term in catalyst deactivation prevention. It's unclear how this would address poisoning specifically.

C. "Limit the transition-state shape selectivity" - Shape selectivity is related to how molecules fit into catalyst pores. Limiting this would likely reduce catalyst effectiveness rather than prevent poisoning.

D. "Operate at higher reaction temperatures" - Higher temperatures can help overcome catalyst poisoning by increasing desorption rates of poisons or providing enough energy to maintain activity despite some active sites being poisoned.

E. "Use egg-shell catalyst particles" - Egg-shell catalysts have the active component concentrated on the outer shell of the particle, which can help when dealing with poisoning by limiting poison penetration.

Based on my analysis, option C seems least likely to solve catalyst deactivation by poisoning. Limiting transition-state shape selectivity would likely reduce catalyst effectiveness rather than prevent poisoning. In fact, it might make the catalyst more susceptible to poisoning by allowing more types of molecules to interact with active sites.
